Title: Stochastic Data Envelopment Analysis—A review - ScienceDirect
We discuss extensions of deterministic DEA in three directions: (i) deviations from the deterministic frontier are modeled as stochastic variables, (ii) random noise in terms of measurement errors, sample noise, and specification errors is made an integral part of the model, and (iii) the frontier is stochastic as is the underlying Production Possibility Set (PPS). Measuring the relative efficiency and ranking productive performance of Decision Making Units (DMUs) were originally the primary purpose of the Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) proposed in Charnes, Cooper, and Rhodes (1978) and Banker, Charnes, and Cooper (1984). By Stochastic DEA we mean an efficiency analysis using non-parametric convex hull/convex cone reference technologies based on either statistical axioms or distributional assumptions that allow for a random (estimator of the) reference technology.1 As noted by Banker (1996), the original DEA formulations assume that the included inputs and outputs are measured without noise, and do not forward any axioms on the distributional structure of deviations from a best practice frontier. Banker (1993) shows that DEA (with one output) provides a consistent estimator of the best practice frontier as a piecewise linear monotonically increasing and concave production function, if one is willing to accept the following two additional axioms: (i) the deviations from the frontier are iid distributed on a one-sided support (only negative residuals are allowed in an output oriented model with one output and multiple inputs), and (ii) the corresponding density function is monotonically decreasing in the absolute size of the residuals. These successful interpretations of DEA inspired models as a semi-parametric estimation procedure of a stochastic frontier have clearly narrowed the gap between the DEA and the SFA approach for efficiency and productivity analysis. results.title: Understanding Stochastic Frontier Analysis: Estimating Efficiency with Random Errors
results.content:
Title: Understanding Stochastic Frontier Analysis: Estimating Efficiency with Random Errors
Understanding Stochastic Frontier Analysis: Estimating Efficiency with Random Errors. # Understanding Stochastic Frontier Analysis: Estimating Efficiency with Random Errors. Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) is a robust statistical method that plays a crucial role in measuring production efficiency. One of the key advantages of SFA is its ability to handle random errors effectively, a feature that sets it apart from other efficiency estimations such as Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA). While DEA is a non-parametric method that constructs a piecewise linear frontier to evaluate efficiency, it does not incorporate stochastic noise, potentially conflating random variations with inefficiency. In contrast, SFA incorporates a probabilistic error term, separating inefficiency effects from random shocks, thus offering a more refined analysis. Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) is grounded in the theoretical concept of measuring the efficiency of productive units, incorporating random errors and inefficiencies. A key feature of SFA is the stochastic production frontier, a mathematical model that represents the highest attainable level of output given a set of inputs, factoring in the potential for random deviations. Through these mathematical representations, SFA provides a robust framework for evaluating efficiency, disentangling inefficiencies from random noise, and offering insights into the performance of productive entities. The stochastic frontier model is a sophisticated econometric approach that separates inefficiency from random errors in the analysis of productivity and cost behaviors. Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) relies on various estimation techniques to measure efficiency while accounting for random errors. Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) has found applications across a wide array of industries, offering valuable insights into efficiency measurement and improvement. By incorporating random errors into efficiency estimation, SFA addresses the innate variability present in different sectors, making it an adaptable tool for varied application. Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) aims to estimate the efficiency of decision-making units (DMUs), commonly firms or industries, considering the presence of random errors. In sum, interpreting SFA results requires a nuanced examination of efficiency scores, statistical significance, and the separation of true inefficiency from random noise. Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) is a powerful tool for estimating efficiency, but it is not without its challenges and limitations. For SFA to be effective, it is crucial to correctly specify the functional form of the production frontier and the distribution of inefficiency effects.
